idiom_name: oneTBB task_group / parallel_reduce with TBB's work-stealing scheduler
implementation_notes: Modern C++ answers fork/join with a task-parallel runtime instead of raw threads: oneTBB's task_group.run() forks tasks and wait() joins them, parallel_invoke/parallel_for/parallel_reduce express the common bulk shapes, and the TBB scheduler keeps per-thread task pools and lets idle threads participate, so the classic deque/stealing logic is never written by hand. C++17's <execution> parallel algorithms are a lighter option when the recursion can be phrased as a range algorithm, and C++26 std::execution (senders/receivers) is the standard-library successor with when_all/bulk for dynamic fan-out. Hand-rolled std::thread pools with deques are justified only where no runtime may be linked or a fixed platform API must be spoken.
pitfalls: Nested task groups or parallel_for calls inside an already-parallel region oversubscribe the machine - oneTBB is one global pool, so do not create additional pools.
Captured references must outlive the tasks; g.wait() must run inside the scope before the referenced locals die.
Blocking (I/O, locks, condition waits) inside TBB tasks throttles the scheduler - the runtime is tuned for compute-bound tasks.

variants.name: OpenMP task/taskgroup (compiler runtime)
variants.idiom_name: #pragma omp task + taskgroup over the OpenMP worker team
variants.implementation_notes: The OpenMP route treated as C++: spawn the team once, let #pragma omp task fork subtasks and #pragma omp taskgroup join the child tasks and their descendants. It compiles with the same C++ toolchain and needs no library, which makes it the pragmatic choice in HPC code and on toolchains where adding TBB is not an option; the cost is pragma-based error checking and explicit data-sharing discipline (shared by default, reduction/task_reduction for leaf results).
pitfalls: Data-sharing clauses decide correctness: shared is the default, so leaf results need reduction/task_reduction or firstprivate captures.
Forgetting taskgroup means the parent can read results before child tasks wrote them.
OpenMP task overhead is higher than TBB's; keep the granularity threshold generous in hot loops.

variants.name: C++26 std::execution sender/receiver task graph
variants.idiom_name: std::execution::bulk / when_all over a parallel scheduler
variants.implementation_notes: C++26 standardizes the sender/receiver model (P2300): describe the work as a composable task graph - bulk() fans a shape out over a scheduler, when_all() is the join - and connect/start it; the executor decides the threads. A parallel scheduler (plus when_all) is the standard-library replacement for a hand-owned pool; the sender graph additionally carries cancellation and error channels, which is exactly the structured-join discipline the pattern wants. Adopt when the toolchain implements it; until then oneTBB or OpenMP remain the practical choices.
pitfalls: Only a parallel scheduler provides parallelism; an inline scheduler completes on the calling thread.
Senders are single-shot: connect exactly once and keep the operation state alive until it signals completion.
Through as_awaitable the completing thread is not necessarily the awaiting one - do not assume the caller's context resumes the coroutine.
